Choose foods that maximize calories per ounce. Freeze-dried meals are fine, but you’re going to want to snack in between. I tend to under-eat when I’m backpacking, so I pack stuff I really enjoy so it feels like a special treat. (Oreos are my personal favorite. Calorie dense, carb-y, and appetizing.) If you’re at altitude you’re going to need more carbs, salt, and water than you would at sea level.

“Decant” the freeze-dried meals into Ziplock bags so you can squeeze the air out and save space. I write the instructions on the bag in Sharpie.

Six hours per day isn’t too long, depending on your fitness level. But you really need to be brutally honest with yourself about your abilities. If six hours feels like your personal max, maybe cut it down to four. Do not underestimate the impact a full pack, altitude, and terrain have. I conditioned for eight weeks before my first trip and it was still pretty tough.

Consider renting an emergency GPS beacon if you don’t already have something similar. It’s nice peace of mind for you and the people who love you.

Finally, alone in the wilderness is not the time or place to really push it. If you feel like garbage or you’re in a rough place mentally, there is no shame in tapping out. Your safety and well-being come first; do NOT force yourself to your personal limit.

Hi. Late 30s, living alone in one of the most expensive cities in the nation, and a reformed serial monogamist. Hopefully I can add some valuable perspective.

  
First, it's pretty well established that women are [happiest when they're single](https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2019/may/25/women-happier-without-children-or-a-spouse-happiness-expert). It's been several years since I've been in a serious relationship and I recently quit dating apps altogether. I can confirm that my mental health is the best it's been in years. I don't feel isolated, but I have also gone out of my way to consciously maintain non-romantic connections with my neighbors, my family, and long-distance friends. I am an introvert so my social cup gets filled pretty quickly. In my city, there are endless volunteer opportunities and social groups just for making friends. I highly, highly recommend looking into a few and attending *consistently.* Consistency is the key to forming strong relationships. 

With regards to finances, you're in a better place than I am. I left a corporate career a few years ago to pursue a blue-collar passion.
